claims.text: Tungsten particles will receive an ultrathin nanoscale silver coating before W–Cu composite consolidation.
The silver coating will form an interlayer at tungsten–copper interfaces.
The silver interlayer will improve bonding between the tungsten and copper phases.
The silver interlayer will improve connectivity between the tungsten and copper phases.
Silver coating of tungsten will improve the wettability of tungsten by copper.
Silver coating of tungsten will reduce thermal boundary resistance between the tungsten and copper phases.
Reduced interfacial thermal resistance will enhance phonon and electron transfer across W–Cu interfaces.
The silver-coated W–Cu composite will have higher effective thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable composite made with untreated tungsten particles.
The silver-coated composite will retain mechanical properties comparable to those of the uncoated W–Cu baseline.
The silver-coated composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to that of the uncoated W–Cu baseline.
The silver interlayer will not alter the intrinsic durability of the constituent phases.
The silver interlayer will not alter the intrinsic irradiation response of the constituent phases.

The predicted benefit should hold under conventional sintering or infiltration and under high-heat-flux and irradiation service conditions typical of heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity increase will depend on silver-layer thickness, coating uniformity, and interface quality after consolidation.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant thermal-conductivity increase, or measurable degradation of mechanical durability or irradiation resistance, will falsify the hypothesis.
